doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

chapter: Race, audiences and the jazz scene
title: Racial makeup of jazz festivals and stratification of the music
summary: He ties mostly white festivals to jazz's factions, contrasts the enthusiastic Jackie Robinson Foundation event, and urges wider programming.

venues.name: Jackie Robinson Foundation Afternoon for Jazz

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you have an opinion on the racial state of jazz these days? I think of it when I’m at a function like this, that the audience is all white and —
And the bands are all white.

With the exception of one player at this particular festival. And it seems to be the case. The only difference I’ve seen was a jazz cruise that I went on once, and I don’t know, do you have an indication of why that’s happened?

That’s a very complicated issue. I think it has something to do with the stratification of this music. You know it’s like an oreo cookie that people are always trying to take apart and just get at one layer of it somehow. You know there’s so many different factions and different camps, and well there’s got to be classic jazz, and well how do we define that, well it’s got to be this or that, it’s got to be like Chicago school or it’s got to be Oliver- Armstrong-Hardin thing or the Austin High gang, or it’s got to be the Condon thing. And then you’ve got the bebop faction and what they call the avante garde and it’s all so stratified. And everybody’s trying to pick out a certain layer of it and sweep all the others aside. And I think that must have something to do with it. Because at these kind of events the entire spectrum of the music is not really presented of course. It’s a quote unquote mainstream traditional/mainstream segment of the music. And I think that maybe the black audiences are not attracted to that. The black audiences are certainly there. I mean I’ve played at the Jackie Robinson Foundation, Afternoon for Jazz which is held annually, and that was one of the best times I ever had at a festival. I did it this year also, but I did it two years ago. This year it was with Thelonious Monk Jr. and two years ago it was Frank Wess’s band with Frank Foster as a guest soloist, and I don’t know how many people were there but just a huge sea of people, almost all black people. And they are very, very enthusiastic and very, very happy to hear this music. And they come up and they say, “Thank you — thank you for coming here and playing this music for us. We hunger for this, this is just great.” And many of the performers were black. But they treated us so nicely. They had all this great food — collard greens and yams and all of that, and they’re like, “Oh can we carry your instruments?” We were fantastically well treated and I remember leaving there and this woman came up and said, “Please come back, please. You come back here and play for us again.” And I had just come from an event, more of this genre, and I felt like everybody was kind of like apathetic. I’m not talking about this event.
Yeah, I know what you mean.

I’ll leave the event unnamed. But everything was white, all the musicians were white, all the audience was white, the music clung to a relatively narrow band of the spectrum of © Hamilton Fillius Archive -10-

jazz possibilities, it was very safe, and I felt like okay, now there’s a lesson to be learned here somewhere, you know? Is it possible that we could make these events more inclusive, and present a little wider spectrum of the music and bring more people into it and maybe people from this kind of camp would discover that hey, this stuff’s pretty good and people from that kind of camp would say hey, you know. I would like to have things mixed up a little bit. A little of this then a little of that, and I’m not afraid of being shocked or of shocking people. So I don’t know, I think it might be possible to present a little wider spectrum and have a more balanced audience.
